history.summary: CSV TOWN FLAG: Sikkim's famous Thakurbari temple is on M.G. Marg in central GANGTOK, not in Tadong. 'Thakurbari' is a common generic name (shrines of that name exist in Bihar, West Bengal, Meghalaya and Bangladesh), but in a Sikkim list the only well-supported referent is Shri Thakurbari Temple, Gangtok - documented here with the corrected location. Tadong is a suburb ~5 km east of central Gangtok, so the CSV town is approximate at best; no separate Thakurbari temple at Tadong could be located. Built in 1935 on land donated by King Thutob Namgyal of Sikkim, the temple is described as one of the oldest Hindu temples in Gangtok. It was further extended into a major religious complex in 1945-1947, housing all major deities and serving as the point of convergence for Hindus in Gangtok; further upgrades including a multi-purpose hall and library are reportedly planned (verify). Chhath Puja, dedicated to the Sun god Surya, is celebrated lavishly here. The temple sits ~170 m from M.G. Marg in the heart of the city.

name: Thakurbari Temple
town: Gangtok (CSV town 'Tadong' is WRONG - Sikkim's famous Thakurbari is on M.G. Marg in central Gangtok; no separate Thakurbari at Tadong could be located)
town_description: Gangtok, Sikkim's capital (population ~100,000), sits at ~1,650 m on the Himalayan foothills. The Thakurbari temple lies in the heart of the city on M.G. Marg, Gangtok's main pedestrian promenade, about 170 m from the mall road and easily reachable on foot from the city centre. Tadong, the CSV town, is a suburb ~5 km east along NH-10.

travel.airport: Pakyong Airport - about 30 km (verify); Bagdogra is the main gateway.
travel.road: In the heart of Gangtok on M.G. Marg, ~170 m from the mall road; walkable from the city centre; taxis and shared vehicles (verify).

visitor_information.best_time: September to November and March to May (pleasant weather); October-November brings the Chhath Puja fervour.
visitor_information.opening_hours: Widely reported as 6:00 AM-8:00 PM daily (verify). Photography is strictly not allowed inside the temple without prior consent of the priests.
